title: Key takeaways: Detroit Lions finalize initial 53-man roster
summary: Following the quick turnaround from the final preseason game, general manager Brad Holmes and head coach Dan Campbell have finalized the Detroit Lions’ initial 53-man roster. Below are my three key takeaways. Jahmyr Gibbs: Offensive Weapon The Lions surprisingly cut down to only 4 wide receivers while keeping five running backs on the initial roster. […]
full_text: Following the quick turnaround from the final preseason game, general manager Brad Holmes and head coach Dan Campbell have finalized the Detroit Lions’ initial 53-man roster. Below are my three key takeaways. Jahmyr Gibbs: Offensive Weapon The Lions surprisingly cut down to only 4 wide receivers while keeping five running backs on the initial roster. My biggest takeaway is that this may signal the Lions are finally cashing in on the Brad Holmes “Jahmyr Gibbs Offensive Weapon” promise. “We thought he was a multiphase, elite, explosive position-less weapon.” Of course, the practice squad has yet to form, and the staff could choose to have five wide receivers active on gamedays by way of elevation, but the unexpected release of gadget wide receiver Greg Dortch gives evidence to the idea that any non-Amon-Ra St. Brown slot snaps are already accounted for. No disrespect to Dortch or any of the other wide receivers competing for a roster spot this training camp, but the reality is that Gibbs presents a far greater matchup problem in the slot than anyone else. Offensive coordinator Drew Petzing explained , “Because the key is the matchups. When you have guys that can do a lot of different things, you can start to dictate things based on what the defense wants to do.” If true, the utilization of a position-less Gibbs could pay dividends with and without the football by dictating defensive personnel and matchups. All-in on a movement-centric defensive line I like the way you move. The Lions opted not to carry a single true nose tackle on the roster after waiving DT Chris Smith. The decision leaves the defense with a group of versatile, athletic pieces to use along the front. While surprising, t he breadcrumbs have been leading in this direction all offseason . The interior of the defensive line now consists of Alim McNeill, Tyleik Williams, Levi Onwuzurike, Skyler Gill-Howard, and Mekhi Wingo. All five linemen possess the versatility to play multiple roles, but more importantly, have the athleticism to execute movement games through stunts and stems. Defensive coordinator Kelvin Sheppard appears to have made this a focal point of his vision for the defense this season. The dynamic traits of the defensive line also help in the pass rush game through designed stunts. Most notably, Wingo was used in multiple unique ways this preseason. I like fun ways to generate pressure. pic.twitter.com/fAyPLJZ3b3 — Jeremy Reisman (@DetroitOnLion) August 30, 2026 Above, as Jeremy Reisman breaks down, Wingo (94) in the 4i- technique over the Indianapolis Colts’ right tackle stunts all the way across to pick the left guard, as the Lions’ opposite end Eric O’Neill loops inside to generate the pressure. Below, Wingo is asked to flash his rush, then drop into coverage. This holds the center’s attention enough to give Skyler Gill-Howard space for an inside rip through the left guard and to the quarterback for a sack. Sky LOCO 😤 pic.twitter.com/53huI3Foac — Detroit Lions (@Lions) August 29, 2026 The new style of defensive front has already shown some positive results this preseason. How Sheppard opts to utilize this skill set will be something to track over the course of the season. Passion plus perseverance pays off Dan Campbell put it best in his postgame presser in Indianapolis after the last preseason game: “It’s an exciting time and it’s also kind of a somber time.” For my final takeaway, I want to focus on the former and put a spotlight on this exciting time for two players in particular. Those guys are defensive end Ahmed Hassanein and tight end Jackson Meeks. Both Hassanein and Meeks are excellent examples of “grit” and why they are perfect for Dan Campbell’s Detroit Lions. First, Hassanein had a rough start to his rookie year after tearing his pectoral muscle, which led to an injury settlement after he was waived, with the expectation that he would sign to the practice squad once healthy. From that point forward, Hassanein appeared to be on a mission , ultimately leading to a transformative offseason where he dropped his body fat from 35 percent to 18 percent . Now, Hassanein is not only the first Egyptian-born athlete to be drafted in the NFL, but he’s the first Egyptian to make an active 53-man NFL roster. Jackson Meeks also deserves his moment. Meeks started his NFL career as an UDFA wide receiver in 2025. But while on the practice squad late in the 2025 season, the Lions started trying Meeks at tight end. From the 213 pounds he was listed at in his NFL draft profile, Meeks has transformed himself into a tight end weighing in at 235 pounds entering training camp. His growth this offseason and effort on special teams earned him a spot on the roster. Hassanein and Meeks are hardly the only players on this Lions team with passion and perseverance. In fact, the team is full of these stories, and that is no accident. Ultimately, the NFL is a game of attrition. A season of highs and lows. When a team is led not only by the likes of Penei Sewell and Amon-Ra St. Brown, but is bookended by Ahmed Hassanein and Jackson Meeks, its identity is one of extreme passion and perseverance. It’s a team that takes on the identity of this city. It’s a team this fan base can be proud of. Sound familiar?

title: Discussion: What was the Detroit Lions’ most surprising roster decision?
summary: The Detroit Lions have set their initial 53-man roster, and it has a fair number of surprises. From unexpected veterans getting cut to players beating the odds and making the team, the Lions made cut-down day entertaining as usual (albeit very delayed—please be quicker with your roster announcement next time!). There is no shortage of […]
full_text: The Detroit Lions have set their initial 53-man roster, and it has a fair number of surprises. From unexpected veterans getting cut to players beating the odds and making the team, the Lions made cut-down day entertaining as usual (albeit very delayed—please be quicker with your roster announcement next time!). There is no shortage of stunning moves that Detroit made , but which decision surprised you the most? Today’s Question of the Day is: What was the Detroit Lions’ most surprising roster decision? My answer: Keeping Jabari Small on the 53-man roster. I will credit Small for making an impact in camp, but that sadly never materialized in preseason. He missed the first preseason game with a knee injury. After just three carries, he suffered a concussion in the second preseason game. In the third and final preseason game, he was knocked out of the game on a kickoff return. It is an unfortunate circumstance for a player who was reportedly neck-and-neck with Jacob Saylors , but the writing was seemingly on the wall for Small. His staying on the roster tells me three things. Firstly, his injury is not severe enough to warrant a stint on the Injured Reserve—the Lions only used one of their two IR-to-return slots on cutdown day (Cade Mays). Second, the team clearly liked him a lot despite his preseason absences. As a shifty player who can contribute as a pass catcher and on special teams, it’s not hard to envision why the Lions would want to keep him around. Finally, you have to wonder about the status of Isiah Pacheco for Week 1 if the Lions are keeping five running backs on the initial roster. While I am still scratching my head about keeping Small over, say, Nick Whiteside, I am happy for Small and excited to see what he can bring to the offense. So, what Lions’ decision was the most surprising to you? Let us know in the comments.

title: Who will be the Packers’ third quarterback?
summary: The Green Bay Packers don’t have a third quarterback, and that’s weird. Half of the NFL kept three players at the position (four of them kept four, if you can believe it) at the cutdown deadline, when rosters shrank from 91 to 53 on Sunday. So for the Packers to have only rostered two players […]
full_text: NASHVILLE, TENNESSEE - AUGUST 29: Miller Moss #16 of the Chicago Bears looks to pass during the second half of a pre-season game against the Tennessee Titans at Nissan Stadium on August 29, 2026 in Nashville, Tennessee. (Photo by Justin Ford/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Green Bay Packers don’t have a third quarterback, and that’s weird. Half of the NFL kept three players at the position (four of them kept four, if you can believe it) at the cutdown deadline, when rosters shrank from 91 to 53 on Sunday. So for the Packers to have only rostered two players at the position and have no internal option to even add to the practice squad sticks out like a sore thumb, but that’s the offset when the Miami Dolphins are willing to give you a draft pick for a guy you signed off the street in January . I’m sure a lot of you are thinking, “Wait, who am I going to see under center if Jordan Love or Tyrod Taylor ever go down, God forbid?” I don’t know the answer to that, but I’m going to throw a couple of options out for you today. Bring back Kyron Drones This is probably the least inspired of our options. The Packers signed Kyron Drones to a deal worth $5,000 guaranteed as an undrafted free agent this offseason, and he was beat out for the QB3 job (at least in the summer) by Kyle McCord (who, again, is now a Dolphin). Drones was outright waived by the team — with the Packers not even needing to fill his roster spot for several days — after a four-dropback performance against the Pittsburgh Steelers in the preseason opener. Drones was sacked on three of those plays, including a screen. It seemed like they were just over the experience. Sign a player who was just cut Alright, here’s where I did a lot of legwork. We’re going to have to use different fonts to mean different things, because I want you to be able to take one glance and understand the full landscape at the position. Players whose names are bolded were cut from teams that kept three or more quarterbacks. These are the players who are most likely to be available for the Packers, as these teams are less likely to need a practice squad arm for the scout team. Players who are italicized come from teams that have only two quarterbacks on the 53-man roster, but there were multiple quarterbacks cut on Sunday. These teams will likely try to re-sign one of them on the practice squad, but not both quarterbacks. Players who are not bolded or italicized come from teams that only kept two quarterbacks on the roster but only released one on Sunday, meaning they’re more likely to be retained by their original team’s practice squad as a camp arm. Given the option, quarterbacks in the #3 spot in the pecking order tend to return to their original club on the practice squad. Below is a full list of all of the quarterbacks cut league-wide (without an injury designation) on Sunday. ARZ: Kedon Slovis BAL: Austin Reed BUF Shane Buechele [update: Buffalo signed Buechele to practice squad] CAR: Kyle Trask CHI: Miller Moss CIN: Sean Clifford [update: Cincinnati signed Clifford to practice squad] DET: Luke Altmyer [update: Detroit signed Altmyer to practice squad] HOU: Brett Rypien IND: Easton Stick [update: Tampa Bay has signed Stick to practice squad] JAX: Nick Mullens and Joey Aguilar [update: Jacksonville signed both Mullens and Aguilar to practice squad] LV: Jacob Clark LAC: DJ Uiagalelei [update: Chargers signed Uiagalelei to practice squad] MIA: Mark Gronowski and Cam Miller [update: Miami signed Gronowski to practice squad] NO: Hunter Dekkers NYG: Brandon Allen and Jake Haener [update: New York signed Haener to practice squad] NYJ: Bailey Zappe and Brady Cook [update: Miami claimed Cook, New York reported to have signed Zappe to practice squad] SF: Adrian Martinez TB: Jake Browning and Connor Bazelak TEN: Will Levis and Hendon Hooker [update: Tennessee signed Hooker to practice squad] WAS: Sam Hartman [update: Washington signed Hartman to practice squad] This draft cycle, I reported that scouting sources told me the Packers were interested in Kyron Drones, Haynes King and Mark Gronowski as potential pickups. Drones had his stint in Green Bay, while Gronowski ended up in Miami (where he took a pre-draft visit) and King actually made Carolina’s 53-man roster as a UDFA (good for him). For perspective, King signed for $210,000 guaranteed compared to Drones’ $5,000. Ultimately, King was just in a different market than Drones when they were both free agents post-draft. So Gronowski is a good start for a watch list, but Miami might retain him. If they do, though, that will likely free up Cam Miller, who was a sixth-round pick in the 2026 draft. Maybe he’s an option, too. Along with King, Jalon Daniels and Jack Strand were UDFA quarterbacks who received large guarantees this offseason and ended up making their team’s initial 53-man roster. A couple who were just cut, though, are Luke Altmyer, Joey Aguilar and Miller Moss. Altmyer, who the Packers had a pre-draft virtual meeting with, will likely be kept by the Detroit Lions, as they only have two quarterbacks on their roster. Aguilar could be available, as the Jacksonville Jaguars have two quarterbacks and released two today. Moss will almost certainly be available, as the Chicago Bears kept three quarterbacks on their 53-man roster. I’m not sure that Will Levis will pass through waivers unclaimed, but if he does, I think his addition would make a lot of sense for the Packers. It seems like both he and the Titans just want to move on, and that he won’t be brought back to Tennessee. If for whatever reason he does return to the Titans, though, that means that they (probably) won’t be bringing back Hendon Hooker, who was a pre-draft visitor with Green Bay before his selection at 68th overall in 2023 by the Detroit Lions. He’s another option that makes some sense. I have no idea how Kedon Slovis (outside of his game against the Packers on Friday) or Adrian Martinez played this preseason, but both of them played in “LaFleur-like” offensive systems, so maybe there would be less friction for them to hit the ground running than a typical outside signing to the practice squad. Those are just a couple of names that I think are realistic right now. A street signing The Packers worked out quarterback Seth Henigan, a UDFA from the class of 2025, this offseason. Green Bay didn’t do a lot of workouts since the start of camp, but they brought him in once, so that’s one possibility. Some veterans are out there, like Jimmy Garoppolo, but it seems highly unlikely that they’d be interested in a practice squad opportunity. I just wouldn’t hold my breath on experience at QB3 this year. Tyrod Taylor has taken care of us in that department. — There’s probably no great answer to QB3 right now, but which of these options do you like better? Let us know in the comments section. My opinion: I think they just grab a scout team arm for now, but if there’s ever a serious injury, I bet they go the veteran route and start looking at Garoppolo and co. on the 53-man roster. For example, last cutdown cycle the team traded a pick for offensive linemen Darian Kinnard and picked up tight end Josh Whyle to the […]
full_text: CANTON, OHIO - AUGUST 06: Trevin Wallace #32 of the Carolina Panthers looks on during the first quarter of the 2026 Pro Football Hall of Fame Game against the Arizona Cardinals at Tom Benson Hall Of Fame Stadium on August 06, 2026 in Canton, Ohio. (Photo by Nick Cammett/Diamond Images via Getty Images) | Diamond Images/Getty Images I’ll keep this one short: The Green Bay Packers target their pre-draft visitors at a high clip, whether it’s the draft, as initial undrafted free agents or further down the line. For example, last cutdown cycle the team traded a pick for offensive linemen Darian Kinnard and picked up tight end Josh Whyle to the practice squad. Whyle eventually ended up winning a roster spot and made this year’s initial 53-man roster . So, who was just made available to the Packers? Good question. So far, these are the players who just hit the market and were brought to Green Bay during their draft cycle (since 2022, when the team started targeting more draft picks). Quarterback Hendon Hooker, Titans (Update: signed with Titans practice squad) Sean Clifford, Bengals (Update: signed with Bengals practice squad) Can I interest anyone in Sean Clifford as a QB3 again? Running Back Velus Jones Jr., Seahawks (Update: signed with Seahawks practice squad) Evan Hull, Cardinals (Update: signed with Cardinals practice squad) Lew Nichols, Steelers (Update: signed with Steelers practice squad) Damon Bankston, Giants The one I’m most interested here is rookie Damon Bankston, who received eight times the guarantees to sign with the New York Giants than the Packers’ UDFA signing Jaden Nixon got this cycle . If Green Bay is pivoting to a more outside zone-based scheme, which has been the indication, I think Bankston fits really well. With that being said, he would probably be a practice squad signing immediately, not a 53-man roster guy. Receiver Anthony Smith, Cowboys (Update: signed with Cowboys practice squad) Samori Toure, Eagles I don’t think the team wants to go down the Samori Toure path again, but rookie receiver Anthony Smith is interesting. Smith was taken two picks after Packers kicker Trey Smack. The seventh-round pick did not make it on the Dallas Cowboys’ roster. He ran a 4.45-second 40-yard dash at 6’2” and 197 pounds. The guy is a speedster. Tight End None Offensive Line Kiran Amegadjie, Bears (Update: Signed with Eagles practice squad ) Esa Pole, Chiefs (Update: Signed with Commanders practice squad ) Both Kiran Amegadjie and Esa Pole are players I could see the Packers adding to the bottom of their offensive line unit. Amegadjie was a third-round pick out of Yale for the Chicago Bears back in 2024, but he never caught on with the team. Esa Pola is a second-year former UDFA who was working with the first-team unit as the team’s left tackle in Kansas City at points this summer, but the Chiefs traded for Diego Pounds right before the cutdown deadline. Defensive Line Eric Johnson II, Falcons With seven interior defensive linemen on the 53-man roster, I’m not sure the Packers even need a practice squad defensive lineman right now. Edge Defender Sam Williams, Cowboys Sam Williams was arrested for felony sexual battery at Ole Miss, but the charges were later dropped. I know now this isn’t a great time to say this , but the Packers bring in a lot of prospects with “off-field” red flags for visits, and they generally do it to rule them out completely. I do not expect Williams to be on Green Bay’s short list. Off-Ball Linebacker Trevin Wallace, Panthers (Update: Claimed by New York Jets ) Here’s an interesting one: Trevin Wallace, the 2024 third-rounder who made 12 starts in 12 games played last year for the Carolina Panthers, was waived by the Panthers today. In total, he played 25 games (20 starts) for Carolina over two regular seasons. I could see the team taking a swing on him. Cornerback D’Arco Perkins-McAllister, Chiefs (Update: Re-signing with Chiefs practice squad ) D’Arco Perkins-McAllister actually started his college career off as a fairly big recruit, but wound up bouncing around schools after two years at TCU. He ended up at New Mexico, UT-Chattanooga and Louisiana-Monroe after that. He was waived by the Kansas City Chiefs, and it’s not like the Packers’ third-team defensive backs played well in the preseason. Maybe they change things up. Safety Jammie Robinson, Falcons Chris Edmonds, Browns Safety is a position that will probably be more impacted on the practice squad level, if anything, than on the 53-man roster level, but two were made available today. Chris Edmonds has played almost exclusively as a special teamer when he’s been active in NFL games in his career, while Jammie Robinson, a former fifth-round pick, is looking to catch on with his sixth team in four years. He’s been available before, and the Packers haven’t added him, so I’m not sure the 25-year-old is going to be a priority for them now.

title: Packers Practice Squad Tracker 2026: Follow all the reports & signings
summary: A 53-man roster isn’t the only thing that NFL teams need to decide on this week. The league’s cutdown deadline from 90 to 53 will come and go on Sunday afternoon, and on Monday it will be time for teams to begin assembling the other major piece of their rosters: the practice squad. Over the […]
full_text: DETROIT, MI - NOVEMBER 27: Green Bay player's helmets sit on the turf during an NFL regular season Thanksgiving Day football game between the Green Bay Packers and the Detroit Lions on November 27, 2025 at Ford Field in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Scott W. Grau/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images A 53-man roster isn’t the only thing that NFL teams need to decide on this week. The league’s cutdown deadline from 90 to 53 will come and go on Sunday afternoon, and on Monday it will be time for teams to begin assembling the other major piece of their rosters: the practice squad. Over the last several years, this component of the roster has expanded greatly in significance. Not long ago, teams could carry a maximum of 8 players on the practice squad, but that number has gradually increased, now doubling to 16 (plus an additional 17th spot if a team signs a player with an international roster exemption). Furthermore, a player can be elevated from the practice squad to the active gameday roster a few times per year without a full promotion to the 53, making the unit a more functional squad of backups and injury replacements. As a result, the NFL has expanded the eligibility rules for practice squads over the years as well. Now, a team can sign players with any level of experience to the squad. At least ten of the 16 spots must be taken up by players with two or fewer years of accrued NFL experience, but that leaves up to six slots that can be filled by players of any experience level. Notably, teams cannot begin signing players to the practice squad until the league’s post-roster cut waivers are processed. That will take place at 12 Noon Central Time on Monday, when waiver claims will be awarded. After that, any players who clear waivers become free agents and are eligible to sign with any team, either to a full 53-man roster spot or to a practice squad. Still, there will be reports during cutdown day on Sunday of players whom the Packers would like to bring back for the practice squad if they do clear waivers. Here, APC will keep track of those reports through Sunday, followed by the actual signings on Monday afternoon. The Green Bay Packers have used the practice squad heavily in recent years as rules have changed, often promoting players to the gameday roster to fill in for injured players or to contribute on special teams. As such, today is an important day for general manager Brian Gutekunst and his staff, who will surely be working hard to bring back several individuals whom the Packers waived as part of Sunday’s cutdown. Building out a deep squad can have a major impact on a team’s ability to withstand challenges over the course of the season, and the quality of players on that unit could be the difference between the Packers going over or under their projected win total of 9.5, which is the current number on FanDuel sportsbook . Keep it here throughout the next day or two as the squad fills out. Reports of Practice Squad Signings The following players have reportedly agreed to sign with the Packers’ practice squad. RB Pierre Strong Jr. WR Isaiah Neyor WR Chris Hilton Jr. TE Drake Dabney OL Dalton Cooper OL Dillon Wade OL Josh Gesky DL Jaden Crumedy ED Nyjalik Kelly ED Arron Mosby LB Kristian Welch CB Domani Jackson S Murvin Kenion III The Packers have four more practice squad spots available. One will likely be used on an outside quarterback signing, while the other needs to be used on an international player pathways program player. Green Bay confirmed their first 13 signings today. They were all players who were retained by the Packers after cutdowns. Reported Practice Squad Targets The Packers have released the following players on Sunday, but the reports of their release have indicated that the Packers intend to or are interested in bringing them back for the practice squad if they clear waivers. OL Dylan Barrett RB Jaden Nixon (update: no longer the case ) S Mark Perry (update: no longer the case ) S Jaylin Simpson (update: no longer the case )

full_text: PITTSBURGH, PENNSYLVANIA - DECEMBER 15: Kaleb Johnson #20 of the Pittsburgh Steelers runs prior to an NFL football game against the Miami Dolphins at Pennsylvania on December 15, 2025 in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Green Bay Packers have added depth to their running back room on Sunday, as they’ve traded for former Pittsburgh Steelers running back Kaleb Johnson. Johnson, a 23-year-old, was a third-round pick for the Steelers coming out of Iowa last season. Johnson ended up buried on Pittsburgh’s dept chart, though, following the team’s signings of Rico Dowdle and Travis Homer behind starter Jaylen Warren. As a rookie, the former All-American carried the ball just 28 times for 69 yards (2.5 yards per attempt) in the regular season, good for the third-most attempts on the team behind Warren and Kenneth Gainwell. Funny enough, he was actually fourth on the Steelers in rushing yards last year, as tight end Jonnu Smith had nine carries for 70 yards and a touchdown. Smith, who previously played for head coach Matt LaFleur when LaFleur was an offensive coordinator for the Tennessee Titans, was signed by the Packers earlier this week . Johnson played 11 snaps of special teams in 10 games, with 8 of those snaps being kickoff returns on which he got his hands on the ball. It doesn’t seem like he has much of a background on teams other than as a kickoff returner, something that will probably go to receivers Skyy Moore and Savion Williams during the regular season. He had a long of 29 yards on his eight returns last year. The Packers have released running back Pierre Strong Jr., according to the Milwaukee Journal Sentinel ’s Tom Silverstein. It looks as though Green Bay will enter the regular season with four backs on its roster: Josh Jacobs, MarShawn Lloyd, Chris Brooks and Johnson. So far, there have been no reports on the compensation that the Steelers will receive for Johnson, be it a player or draft pick. Update: NFL insider Adam Caplan is now reporting that the expected compensation for the Johnson trade is a future sixth-round pick . Update #2: #Packers are giving a 2028 sixth-round pick to the #Steelers for running back Kaleb Johnson, according to a source. The pick is their own and not the one they obtained from Miami. — Tom Silverstein (@TomSilverstein) August 30, 2026 So, the Packers functionally traded QB Kyle McCord for RB Kaleb Johnson. — Update #3: It’s a 7th for Kaleb Johnson. Not a 6th. Even better! pic.twitter.com/iBp4Yat0Id — Andy Herman (@AndyHermanNFL) August 31, 2026 It is actually a seventh-round pick that was given up in the trade, not a sixth-round pick. This is interesting, since both the Packers and Steelers claimed it was a sixth-round pick, not a seventh-round pick. It’s possible this is an error on the league’s part. — Update #4: The compensation for the Kaleb Johnson has been fixed on the wire, by the way. It's a 2028 sixth. pic.twitter.com/nDjoIR8Wdc — weston hodkiewicz (@WesHod) August 31, 2026 The great Kaleb Johnson trade controversy is officially over. The NFL made the mistake and has changed the compensation from a seventh-round pick to a sixth-round pick.

title: Packers Film Room, Preseason Week 3: Sturdivant goes for 6
summary: The final preseason game is in the books, so I’m working to get into regular season shape by doing what I love doing the most: breaking down plays. It’s never quite as interesting in the preseason because the focus of the offense isn’t on sequencing in the same way we see in the regular season. […]
full_text: GREEN BAY, WISCONSIN - AUGUST 28: J. Michael Sturdivant #87 of the Green Bay Packers scores a touchdown during the second quarter of a preseason game against the Arizona Cardinals at Lambeau Field on August 28, 2026 in Green Bay, Wisconsin. (Photo by Geoff Stellfox/Getty Images) | Getty Images The final preseason game is in the books, so I’m working to get into regular season shape by doing what I love doing the most: breaking down plays. It’s never quite as interesting in the preseason because the focus of the offense isn’t on sequencing in the same way we see in the regular season. We don’t get to see how a particular play is built-up over the course of several games. But we got a really fun play this week that we’ll likely see as a pay-off at least once during the regular season. It also involves my preseason crush, J. Michael Sturdivant (who I may have written about once or twice ), so, legally, I have to write about it. So, today, we’re looking at the 29 yard TD pass from Kyle McCord to J. Michael Sturdivant. The Packers are in 11 personnel (1 RB, 1 TE, 3 WR). They start in a 2×2 formation, but Will Sheppard [82] shifts before the snap, putting them in a Nub formation (three receivers to one side and the TE in-line as the only receiving option on the other side). Kyle McCord [18] gives a play action flash-fake to Jaden Nixon [35], then turns left and pumps to the flat. To that side of the field, Isaiah Neyor [80] releases vertically on a post route, J. Michael Sturdivant [87] is showing a stalk-block and Sheppard is releasing to the flat underneath Sturdivant. That action from Sturdivant and Sheppard triggers a response from Quinton Newsome [30]. Newsome is over Sturdivant in the slot, but the combination of stalk-block and flat release makes this look like a WR screen to the outside. Instead, Sturdivant is running a stalk-and-go: fake the stalk block, then release vertically up the sideline. Newsome plays this by splitting the difference. He’s playing on Sturdivant’s inside shoulder and trying to carry him on the route, while putting himself in position to drive down on Sheppard on the screen. With the boundary defender carrying Neyor on the post, Sturdivant easily gets past Newsome and McCord lays a beautiful ball up the sideline before the boundary defender can get back over to defend it. McCord puts his whole body into this throw, man. And it’s a good one. Steps back away from pressure to buy the little extra time, then puts this on a line before the defender can get over the top. This works because it plays off that common WR screen look. The Packers certainly aren’t the only team that runs it, but they run it enough for teams to react to it. It’s something that feels familiar, right up until it’s not. Ultimately, this play helped both McCord and Sturdivant get jobs on active NFL rosters to start the 2026 regular season. Sturdivant made the Packers’ 53 as the 6th wide receiver (with Savion Williams going on injured reserve), while McCord found himself headed to Green Bay south after the Packers traded him to the Miami Dolphins for a future draft pick. Albums listened to: Interpol – This Mirror Weighs a Ton ; DMA’S – DMA’S

summary: It has been an eventful seven days for the Green Bay Packers. full_text: Travis Glover #79 of the Green Bay Packers high-fives a young fan while carrying equipment at the Green Bay Packers training camp at Ray Nitschke Field in Ashwaubenon, Wisconsin, on August 2, 2026. (Photo by Ross Harried/NurPhoto via Getty Images) | NurPhoto via Getty Images It has been an eventful seven days for the Green Bay Packers. Looking back at the chaos of the last few days — between the final preseason game and the roster cut deadline on Sunday — it feels a bit bizarre to remember that the Packers released a new slate of alternate uniforms just six days ago. Those uniforms, part of the NFL’s Rivalries program, got their reveal last Tuesday, and it’s worth revisiting the reaction to them now that it’s in the rear-view mirror. For a refresher, here’s a look at the full new getup, which the Packers will wear at Lambeau Field in their week 5 game against the Chicago Bears: It always has been, and always will be, for the G. pic.twitter.com/RPm9IgyTj8 — Green Bay Packers (@packers) August 25, 2026 While some reactions to the new threads from football fans as a whole were positive , those of Packers fans were somewhat mixed. Therefore, we at Acme Packing Company wanted to get a feel for what the overall feeling is among the fan base. Ready for the results? It was a simple question that we posed: do you love them, hate them, or fall somewhere in between? Thankfully, only a small percentage of fans — just 15 percent — want to fire these new uniforms into the sun. However, a substantial majority at 59 percent are somewhere in the middle, with about a quarter of survey respondents giving a strongly positive reaction. Because of this program, the Packers-Bears rivalry will not see the two teams match up in their normal, classic uniforms this season. Each team will wear its new alternate in its home game against the other, with the Bears donning theirs at Soldier Field in Week 16. Interestingly, FanDuel Sportsbook already has odds available for the meeting in Chicago , with the Bears currently slight 1.5-point favorites to win on Christmas Day. For now, though, we can wait to worry about how the Packers look and play in these alternate uniforms for at least a few more weeks.

title: Jonathan Gannon’s Packers preseason pressure packages
summary: The 2026 preseason has concluded, but the Green Bay Packers’ three games gave us a glimpse into the mind of Jonathan Gannon as the new defensive coordinator gears up for his first season calling the defense. While Gannon called a mostly vanilla preseason, he did throw a couple of interesting blitz calls out in the […]
full_text: PITTSBURGH, PENNSYLVANIA - AUGUST 13: Will Howard #18 of the Pittsburgh Steelers rushes against the Green Bay Packers in the first half at Acrisure Stadium on August 13, 2026 in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Justin K. Aller/Getty Images) | Getty Images The 2026 preseason has concluded, but the Green Bay Packers’ three games gave us a glimpse into the mind of Jonathan Gannon as the new defensive coordinator gears up for his first season calling the defense. While Gannon called a mostly vanilla preseason, he did throw a couple of interesting blitz calls out in the first week of the preseason, giving a glimpse into concepts that we’re likely to see a bit more in regular season games. A coordinator like Gannon has a deep tool belt for generating pressure on opposing quarterbacks, and one of the more unusual concepts he can call is often referred to as “hot quarters coverage.” It’s a rare call, one we’ve seen a few times the last couple of seasons under Jeff Hafley. In the preseason, I charted it only twice but it’s a fascinating way to manufacture pressure precisely because of how much extra communication it forces an offense to handle before the snap. Hot Quarters Pressure The core idea is simple in concept but hard to defend: get the offensive line to slide its protection away from where the real pressure is actually coming from, freeing up a rusher the offense never accounts for. This particular pressure concept was popularized by Brian Flores, defensive mind who built his reputation on manufactured pressure and disguised fronts, and it’s since spread around the league as coordinators borrow pieces of it to create the same problems for opposing quarterbacks and offensive lines. The front is built to bait the protection into sliding fully to one side, with the hope that a rusher comes free away from the overloaded side. Typically, two defenders will “pop out” late from the box into underneath zone coverage, locating and matching the second and third receivers in the pattern from the inside out — that’s the “hot” element the concept is named for. Because so many defenders are stacked on the line pre-snap, the offense is often forced into a full-slide protection scheme to account for numbers, which all but guarantees that one edge defender comes free with no one assigned to him. Any breakdown in protection communication — particularly a missed check on a mugged linebacker showing blitz — puts the quarterback in immediate danger. The stress this concept places on offensive communication comes from the crowded, chaotic pre-snap picture it creates. All that traffic near the line of scrimmage makes it difficult for the offensive line to identify who’s actually rushing and who’s dropping, and that hesitation or miscommunication is exactly what the defense is hunting for. On the back end, the coverage borrows from split-safety, split-field principles. Rather than a traditional two-deep, four-under shell, the coverage defenders play match-quarters technique, matching receivers based on route distribution — corners carrying the first receiver out and vertical, safeties matching the first inside and vertical release. The two pop-out defenders are reading and matching the number two and number three receivers underneath, splitting responsibility between them. In one example of the concept in action, the offensive line slid its protection toward the pop-out defenders, whose late movement pulled the offensive linemen’s eyes and technique with them. That slide left the middle of the protection compromised, and a blitzing linebacker came through almost untouched to pressure the quarterback. The quarterback got rid of the ball in time with a check down to the flat to avoid the sack, but the disguised pressure and coverage combined to hold the play to a modest gain. What makes the concept so effective in short bursts is that it attacks protection rules rather than raw talent — even a well-coached offensive line can get exploited if the pre-snap picture is disguised well enough that their eyes and slide go the wrong direction. Because it’s used so sparingly, it also retains an element of surprise: offenses that haven’t specifically prepared for it in that week’s game plan are far more likely to misidentify it, which may be exactly why coordinators tend to save it for moments when a free rusher would do the most damage. Nickel Fire Zone Pressure Punch is a five-man rush, three-deep/three-under fire zone pressure that sends the nickel back off the edge while simultaneously rushing the backside end. The coverage is a true five-man pressure built around safety rotation into the nickel spot, tagged with a “Ringo/Lucky” call — the signal that tells the front which side the zone pressure is arriving from so the line and second-level rushers can sync their rush lanes and stunts. Because it commits five to the rush, Punch leaves only six defenders in coverage, which is what separates it from the more common “simulated” pressure teams will disguise as fire zones. Where sim pressures often bluff five rushers and drop back into a four-man rush at the snap, Punch actually sends the extra man — making it a genuine, “true” fire zone rather than a pre-snap disguise. What separates the best fire-zone pressures — and what makes the quarters zone pressure and “Punch” effective — comes down to three things: they manipulate protection rules (forcing the offensive line into bad slide or gap-exchange decisions before the snap), they attack the running back in pass protection specifically (since backs are the weak link in most protection schemes against an extra rusher), and they’re timed to exploit the offense’s protection call rather than just adding numbers. A well-disguised, well-timed fire zone doesn’t just outnumber the protection — it wins the answer key before the snap.

title: Houston Texan Wide Receiver Room Update
summary: The Houston Texans are in the process of finalizing their 53-man roster, and one notable name was cut: rookie wide receiver Lewis Bond. Bond received rave reviews throughout the offseason, so it was somewhat surprising to see him not make the initial roster, especially considering the injuries Houston is dealing with in the wide receiver […]
full_text: CHARLOTTE, NORTH CAROLINA - AUGUST 26: Wide receiver Lewis Bond #82 of the Houston Texans looks on during a joint practice with the Carolina Panthers at Carolina Panthers Practice Fields on August 26, 2026 in Charlotte, North Carolina. (Photo by Matt Kelley/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Houston Texans are in the process of finalizing their 53-man roster, and one notable name was cut: rookie wide receiver Lewis Bond. Bond received rave reviews throughout the offseason, so it was somewhat surprising to see him not make the initial roster, especially considering the injuries Houston is dealing with in the wide receiver room. You could make the argument that Bond did not make a huge impact during the preseason games, which ultimately played a role in the decision to cut him. Either way, the Texans have decided to bring him back, and he is now on their practice squad. It would not be surprising to see Bond active on some game days this season, especially if more injuries begin to pile up. He possesses talent that will be valuable at some point, as he continues to develop. The wide receivers who made the initial 53-man roster are: Nico Collins Kayshon Boutte Jaylin Noel Jared Wayne Xavier Hutchinson Tank Dell has been placed on injured reserve, meaning he will miss at least the first four games of the season. This makes sense considering how slowly the Texans have brought him along throughout his recovery. They are not going to rush him back, and that is absolutely the right move. The goal should be having Dell healthy and ready to contribute when the games matter most. The Texans clearly feel comfortable with their wide receiver room, especially after the addition of Kayshon Boutte from the New England Patriots. Now, only time will tell if this group has enough firepower to make a real difference for Houston’s offense in 2026.

title: Did the Colts make the right move at kicker?
summary: It was one of the more intriguing but not always talked about battles in camp. It went back and forth and dipped into last season’s production to make the call. One showed a lot of promise, the other perfection. That was last year, and this is now. The race was neck and neck, but only […]
full_text: It was one of the more intriguing but not always talked about battles in camp. It went back and forth and dipped into last season’s production to make the call. One showed a lot of promise, the other perfection. That was last year, and this is now. The race was neck and neck, but only one kicker could make the 53-man roster. The Indianapolis Colts put any remaining speculation to bed as they made their choice at kicker by choosing Spencer Shrader over Blake Grupe. Why did they choose Shrader over Grupe? That’s one question. The other? Was it the right decision? Time will tell for the second question with hindsight being 20/20. For the why, while we don’t have all the details, the proof was in the pudding. When the lights turned on, one man showed up while the other went quiet. Grupe was a star in practice, but practice kicks don’t win games. He struggled close and at distance. Even one that went in needed the crossbar’s help. Meanwhile, Shrader demonstrated the ice water in his veins. He added the one piece that was missing from his game; the long ball. His leg didn’t have the necessary strength in 2025. He could convert, but the Colts had to get him closer than they would like. Having a kicker who can trot out and make 60+ yard field goals at a consistent rate is huge. It could be the difference between the playoffs and sitting at home. That’s the confidence the Colts needed. They found it in Shrader. Either man probably would have done well. Blake Grupe’s yips might not have translated over to the regular season. Then again, they might have. Shrader was the kicker before his injury. He cleaned up the deficiencies in his game and demonstrated his ability on the field. That seems like more than enough reason to feel the Colts got it right.

Meanwhile, ex-Indianapolis Colts defensive tackle Colby Wooden was claimed by the New Orleans Saints, while placekicker Blake Grupe was claimed by the New York Jets. Regarding Gushiken, the 5,10”, […]
full_text: FOXBOROUGH, MASSACHUSETTS - AUGUST 22: Kapena Gushiken #34 of the Philadelphia Eagles runs against the New England Patriots during an NFL preseason football game at Gillette Stadium on August 22, 2026 in Foxborough, Massachusetts. (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images Following 53-man roster cuts, the Indianapolis Colts waiver activity has been announced, and the Horseshoe claimed and successfully lander former Philadelphia Eagles defensive back Kapena Gushiken. Meanwhile, ex-Indianapolis Colts defensive tackle Colby Wooden was claimed by the New Orleans Saints, while placekicker Blake Grupe was claimed by the New York Jets. Regarding Gushiken, the 5,10”, 189 pound undrafted rookie defensive back out of Ole Miss spent this offseason with the Philadelphia Eagles. He had 5 tackles (4 solo) in the Eagles preseason opener against the Baltimore Ravens, then 5 tackles (2 solo) versus the New England Patriots, and then 6 tackles (6 solo) against the Cincinnati Bengals in Philadelphia’s recent preseason finale. Projected as a safety/nickelback at the pro level, here’s Gushiken’s NFL.com draft profile : Overview Gushiken is extremely fast with above-average balance and change-of-direction quickness in man coverage. He can stay relatively sticky to routes at all three levels. He does lose track of the clues quarterbacks provide at times, which helps explain his average ball production relative to his athletic ability. He’s compact, tough and willing in run support but will still give way to size on occasion. Overall, Gushiken is scheme-diverse as a nickelback. He has enough cover talent and special-teams value to compete for a roster spot. He had a RAS of 9.16 out of a maximum 10.0 and perhaps, of great importance to the Colts is his recorded 4.35 forty time, which is blazing fast, and will certainly play on their special teams coverage units. Prior to claiming Gushiken, the Colts were carrying only four safeties on their 53-man active roster, having covered five at times in the past, so he’ll be a backup addition to a positional room that also includes Cam Bynum, AJ Haulcy, Hunter Wohler, and Jonathan Owens. It’ll be interesting to see who the Colts waived or placed on the injured reserve list to make extra room for Gushiken. Update (3:24 PM EST): The Colts announced that offensive tackle Luke Tenuta has been waived in a corresponding 53-man active roster move.

title: This isn’t how the Colts wanted Keenan Allen to make headlines
summary: What a debut. Keenan Allen’s name is circulating all around the Circle City, and he has only been in town for a week. Unfortunately, it has nothing to do with his performance in the Indianapolis Colts’ third preseason game. What should have been a forgettable weekend for Allen has turned into front page news. Early […]
full_text: WESTFIELD, IN - AUGUST 20: Indianapolis Colts wide receiver Keenan Allen (10) runs through a drill during the Indianapolis Colts and Atlanta Falcons joint training camp practice on August 20, 2026 at the Grand Park Sports Campus in Westfield, IN. (Photo by Zach Bolinger/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images What a debut. Keenan Allen’s name is circulating all around the Circle City, and he has only been in town for a week. Unfortunately, it has nothing to do with his performance in the Indianapolis Colts’ third preseason game. What should have been a forgettable weekend for Allen has turned into front page news. Early Sunday morning, Allen was arrested for allegedly operating a vehicle while intoxicated. This is a decision that is inadvisable for anyone, not just NFL players. Lives are at risk and serious injury or death could occur. On the lesser side of importance is the fact that a professional athlete finds themselves in any situation like this. It happens way too frequently. For people with millions of dollars, the prevailing question is always, why not call for a ride or have one lined up? For the personal reasons alone, it seems you wouldn’t want to do anything to jeopardize your career. Allen was brought in to be a veteran presence, on and off the field. This is not the example the Colts were hoping he would set out of the gate. Not only is it a terrible look, it could set his team at a disadvantage to start the year. Allen could be looking at a potential three-game suspension. He hurt his team and his reputation, and he could have potentially hurt someone. That is a rough first week on the job. It’s not the type of week most of us would be able to afford. Employment would be on the line in most cases. There’s a good chance this doesn’t affect his job security with the Colts. At the same time, Colts head caoch Shane Steichen isn’t afraid to send a message. Can he afford to though with his job on the line? This sets up an uncomfortable situation for the Colts heading into the season in just a few weeks. Not downplaying what could have been, but it is fortunate no one was seriously hurt. What could be hurt now is Keenan Allen’s image and his new team. No one knows what Allen has to offer the Colts, but they were banking on some production. That production may have to wait a little bit longer.

Practice squad formation rules Teams can begin forming their practice squads after the waiver period expires at 1 p.m. ET on Monday, August 31. The NFL will send a subsequent Personnel Notice confirming the results of the waiver process, and teams can begin signing practice squad players after receiving that notice. A player claimed off waivers cannot go directly to a practice squad. A successful waiver claim means that player goes onto the claiming team’s 53-man roster. The player must first clear waivers before becoming eligible to sign with a practice squad. A standard practice squad consists of 16 players. Teams can have a 17th player if that player qualifies for and is designated under the NFL’s International Player Pathway Program (Jacksonville may keep OL Kilian Zierer in this spot). Players who are not subject to waivers can immediately sign with another team or join a practice squad. Players with four or more accrued seasons are unrestricted free agents when released and are not subject to waivers. Players with three or fewer accrued seasons are subject to the waiver process. He showed enough promise as an undrafted rookie, outplayed some guys on the roster, and looked more valuable long term than some other bubble players that were kept (likely due to draft status).” So, Kansas City is essentially swapping a standout of their own for a standout in San Francisco. If Harris isn’t claimed on waivers, the Chiefs can always bring him back on the practice squad. Either way, Eason’s fit also plays a big role here. Kansas City Chiefs spoil Lane Kiffin, LSU football’s plan of adding NFL linebacker | Yahoo! Sports However, his spot on Kansas City’s 53-man roster likely ends his SEC return plans. Kiffin has openly defended LSU’s decision to pursue players caught between college and professional football. “At the end of the day, because of these rulings, they’re either going to play for you or they’re going to play for someone else around the country,” Kiffin said earlier. In 2024, Brevard earned honorable mention All-Big Ten recognition with 19 tackles, including 5.5 for loss and 1.5 sacks. Chiefs’ Failed Offseason Signing Lands With Division Rival Chargers | Heavy Sports The Chiefs acquired Elam this past spring. It was a typical signing for Veach, who loves to take flyers on former high draft picks who haven’t panned out for other teams. Elam was selected No. 23 overall by the Buffalo Bills in the 2022 NFL Draft. Ironically, the Bills only took Elam because the Chiefs traded up over them to select Trent McDuffie, who Buffalo was hoping to land. Kansas City was hoping to unlock the talent that made Elam a high draft pick, but it didn’t work out. The cornerback room quickly became crowded with young talent, and Elam wasn’t able to separate himself from the pack. The Chargers will be Elam’s fourth team in three years after spending time with the Chiefs, Bills, and Dallas Cowboys. New Chiefs joint real estate venture to develop mixed-use districts in KCK and Olathe | KCTV 5 The Kansas City Chiefs and Hunt Midwest are launching a joint real estate venture called Two-Point Development as they work toward mixed-use districts in both Kansas City, Kansas, and Olathe. The Chiefs announced Monday that the newly-formed company will help shape “vibrant, mixed-use districts around the franchise’s new stadium in Kansas City, Kansas, and new headquarters and training facility in Olathe, Kansas.” Around the NFL Cowboys waive QB Joe Milton, clearing way for Sam Howell to be backup | The Athletic In a surprising move, the Dallas Cowboys waived backup quarterback Joe Milton on Monday, a day after he was on the team’s initial 53-man roster. He struggled a bit in Dallas’ final preseason game Friday after he was outstanding in the first two, but Cowboys coach Brian Schottenheimer said the backup battle between Milton and Sam Howell was “neck-and-neck.” Rams’ Aaron Donald misses practice as planned; return date TBD | ESPN Rams defensive tackle Aaron Donald did not practice Monday, something coach Sean McVay said “was part of the plan all along.” McVay reiterated that he didn’t want to put a timeline on when Donald will play his first game after being retired for two years. But he did not rule out Donald not traveling to Melbourne, Australia, to play in the Rams’ season opener against the San Francisco 49ers on Sept. 10. “Oh, yeah, absolutely,” McVay said when asked whether there was a scenario Donald doesn’t play in Week 1. “That could be a possibility. I wouldn’t rule anything out yet. Undrafted Rookie Jalon Daniels earns Bucs QB2 gig behind Baker Mayfield | NFL.com With a strong training camp and preseason, Daniels leapfrogged Jake Browning and Connor Bazelak for the No. 2 QB gig behind Baker Mayfield. “I’m proud of Jalon,” Mayfield said from his charitable event at Topgolf on Sunday, via the Tampa Bay Times. “I think he’s shown tremendous steps from the first time I met him in the offseason until now. He played his tail off. Worked hard. Worked on the things the coaches wanted to get done out of him and for him to progress with.” In case you missed it on Arrowhead Pride Chiefs Preseason Week 3 snap count analysis Over 13 pass-play snaps against Seattle, rookie wideout Cyrus Allen aligned in the slot 100% of the time, according to Pro Football Focus. He caught just one of the two passes thrown to him, but the usage of Allen in the slot is a continuation of a trend from his time at the University of Cincinnati. In 2025, Allen was in the slot for over 90% of the pass plays in the Bearcats’ offense. In camp, Allen has shown a more well-rounded skill set, but in his rookie year, the offense may focus on using the preseason standout where he is most comfortable and experienced while he develops long-term. During the preseason, we will shorten the analysis, as it is difficult to make definitive statements based on the raw snap-count data. Still, let’s see what we can figure out about the Kansas City Chiefs when taking a closer look at playing time during the 9-9 tie against the Seattle Seahawks last Friday. Starters (offensive): LT Jaylon Moore, LG Kingsley Suamataia, C Creed Humphrey, RG Trey Smith, RT Kahlil Benson, QB Garrett Nussmeier, WR Rashee Rice, WR Xavier Worthy, RB Kenneth Walker, TE Travis Kelce and TE Noah Gray Starters (defensive): DE George Karlaftis, DT Chris Jones, DT Khyiris Tonga, DE Felix Anudike-Uzomah, LB Nick Bolton, LB Jeffrey Bassa, LB Cooper McDonald, S Christian Roland-Wallace, CB Nohl Williams, CB Mansoor Delane, S Jaden Hicks Did not play: QB Patrick Mahomes, QB Justin Fields, QB Chris Oladokun (Concussion), RB Kenneth Walker, WR Jimmy Holiday, LT Josh Simmons (Back), S Chamarri Conner, LB Drue Tranquill (Back spasms), LB Jack Cochrane (Knee), DE Ashton Gillotte (Hamstring), S Alohi Gilman (Low-back spasms), WR Jeff Caldwell (Hyperextended knee), DE Tyreke Smith (Hamstring), G C.J. Hanson, OL Joshua Ezeudu, DE Niles King, DT Omarr Norman-Lott (PUP) The big takeaway Before he made the 53-man roster on Sunday, second-year defensive tackle Marcus Harris was the team’s leader in defensive snaps (42) against Seattle, and he made a big impact in his time on the field. Harris finished the game as the leading tackler, including multiple stops towards the end of the game that preserved the tie. Harris was putting on a strong performance during training camp and the preseason prior to Friday’s finale, but he put the cherry on top of his ascension to the roster against the Seahawks. As things stand right now, he will be the team’s fourth defensive tackle through at least the first four weeks of the season. The Offensive takeaway Over 13 pass-play snaps against Seattle, rookie wideout Cyrus Allen aligned in the slot 100% of the time, according to Pro Football Focus. He caught just one of the two passes thrown to him, but the usage of Allen in the slot is a continuation of a trend from his time at the University of Cincinnati. In 2025, Allen was in the slot for over 90% of the pass plays in the Bearcats’ offense. In camp, Allen has shown a more well-rounded skill set, but in his rookie year, the offense may focus on using the preseason standout where he is most comfortable and experienced while he develops long-term. The Defensive takeaway Veteran cornerback L’Jarius Sneed took the field on the first possession of the game with the starting defense, manning the slot in the team’s Nickel defense. Over six snaps played, Sneed was in the slot for five of them. For most of the preseason, safety Christian Roland-Wallace has aligned as the Nickel defender with the first-team unit. He shifted to a traditional safety role for the preseason finale with injuries to starting safeties Alohi Gilman (Low-back spasms) and Chamarri Conner. It remains to be seen whether Sneed or Roland-Wallace will be the first-team Nickel defender when everyone is healthy, hopefully by Week 1, but it’s clear that the coaching staff trusts Sneed to play multiple roles in the defense; in camp, he was mostly playing outside cornerback while rookie Mansoor Delane was recovering from the shoulder injury. title: Chiefs News: It’s time to form the practice squad
summary: The latest On Sunday, the Kansas City Chiefs revealed the initial 53-man roster, subject to change by the time Week 1 arrives. On Monday, after Noon Arrowhead time, waived players who were unclaimed will become eligible to sign to the practice squad. The Chiefs have 16 spots to fill. Andrew Armstrong and 8 more roster […]
full_text: Kansas City Chiefs general manager Brett Veach, left, and head coach Andy Reid speak while observing players during practice at Chiefs training camp on July 17, 2024, in St. Joseph, Missouri. (Emily Curiel/The Kansas City Star/Tribune News Service via Getty Images) The latest On Sunday, the Kansas City Chiefs revealed the initial 53-man roster, subject to change by the time Week 1 arrives. On Monday, after Noon Arrowhead time, waived players who were unclaimed will become eligible to sign to the practice squad. The Chiefs have 16 spots to fill. Andrew Armstrong and 8 more roster cuts the Kansas City Chiefs should bring back on the practice squad for 2026 | A to Z Sports WR Andrew Armstrong The good news about the Chiefs’ release of Armstrong is that it’s rare for wide receivers to be claimed during 53-man roster cuts. It’s disappointing because it felt like he really earned a roster spot through his play on the field. He led the team in the preseason with 7 receptions for 85 yards. His blocking was about as impressive as it gets. Plus, he’s just a different style and body type than anything else on the roster. Chiefs roster cuts: Five notable players who did not make the team | KMBC 9 Emari Demercado, RB: Demercado is the odd man out in a suddenly crowded running back room. He signed a one-year deal during the offseason, but rookie running back Emmett Johnson and second-year running back Brashard Smith were able to beat him out for roster spots. The Chiefs also kept Remigio, who is mainly used as a returner, closing perhaps another door for Demercado to make the team. Chiefs cut offensive lineman who started four games for them last season | The Kansas City Star Pole played with the second unit during training camp, and actually received snaps with the first team as recently as this summer during organized team activities. The release came Sunday. But the shaky ground came a day earlier. The Chiefs traded a 2028 conditional sixth-round pick to the Ravens for tackle Diego Pounds, a 23-year-old undrafted free agent. His addition left Pole as the odd man out. The Chiefs cut Pole out of training camp a year ago as an undrafted free agent — but they later added him back to their roster. He started the final four games of the season. Three shocking omissions from the Chiefs final 53-man roster announcement | FanSided Kader Kohou I largely expected Kohou not to make the team over the past few weeks. The coaches didn’t seem too interested in putting him in the preseason games until very late, and when in, Kohou failed to separate himself. His role was meant to be the starting slot corner when the Chiefs signed him. But this summer has brought multiple names up in the conversation for the same role. Kohou, who is still recovering from a torn ACL last season, never realized the opportunity in front of him and sadly may have left his most meaningful football behind. Projecting Chiefs Depth Chart After Initial 53-Man Roster Revealed With Several Surprises | Heavy Sports The Chiefs also placed wide receiver Jimmy Holiday on injured reserve and defensive tackle Omarr Norman-Lott on the physically unable to perform list. Changes can still come through waiver claims and additional moves, something general manager Brett Veach made clear before the deadline when he described Kansas City’s roster as not yet a “finished product.” For now, however, the initial 53 provides enough information to project how Andy Reid’s depth chart could look. Around the NFL Aaron Donald back: Three-time Defensive Player of the Year returning to Rams for 2026 season | CBS Sports “If the wife wasn’t happy it wasn’t gonna get done,” Donald said after signing. “My wife was on board and she was with me 100%.” The comeback is now firmly in motion with Donald set to join forces with Garrett in a defensive front that, on paper, is as formidable as any in recent years. Sean McVay wouldn’t commit to Donald playing in Week 1. Packers RB Josh Jacobs placed on commissioner exempt list | ESPN The move comes three days after Jacobs was formally charged with two misdemeanors stemming from an alleged incident with a woman in May. It means Jacobs will not be on the Packers’ 53-man roster and cannot practice or attend games. He will be paid and, with the team’s permission, is allowed to be at the facility for meetings, individual workouts, medical treatments and other non-football activities. Broncos’ Jonathon Cooper placed on NFL commissioner exempt list after June arrests | The Athletic Cooper will be paid his full salary while on the exempt list, but he can’t play in games or practice with the team. He will be allowed to attend meetings and receive treatment at the team facility. Commissioner Roger Goodell has sole discretion to place a player on the list or remove them from it. The exemption is typically used for players who have pending legal cases and/or are still under investigation by the league. The duration of time players spend on the exempt list has ranged from a few days to an entire season, and there’s no indication yet as to how long Cooper could remain on the list. He could still be subject to a suspension by the NFL. In case you missed it on Arrowhead Pride Chiefs’ Omarr Norman-Lott to begin 2026 season on PUP list Harris has arguably earned the spot regardless of Norman-Lott’s health. He finished the preseason with a standout performance against the Seattle Seahawks, stifling multiple handoffs in the backfield and forcing a lengthy field-goal attempt that was ultimately missed. Once Norman-Lott is healthy, it will be interesting to see how the rotation adjusts to welcome him back. For now, Harris looks to compete for snaps with rookie Peter Woods behind defensive tackles Chris Jones and Khyiris Tonga. title: Chargers come in at No. 14 in post-cutdown NFL power rankings
summary: Sunday brought with it the initial iterations of all 32 NFL teams. History tells us none of them are set in stone, even for a single day, before changes start occurring all across the league. But in that very moment following the cutdown, ESPN took to updated their power rankings based on the massive day […]
full_text: INGLEWOOD, CALIFORNIA - AUGUST 20: Justin Herbert #10 of the Los Angeles Chargers warms up before the preseason game against the San Francisco 49ers at SoFi Stadium on August 20, 2026 in Inglewood, California. (Photo by Luke Hales/Getty Images) | Getty Images Sunday brought with it the initial iterations of all 32 NFL teams. History tells us none of them are set in stone, even for a single day, before changes start occurring all across the league. But in that very moment following the cutdown, ESPN took to updated their power rankings based on the massive day of transactions. The Chargers somehow did not see any movement from their post-draft power rankings as they stayed put at No. 14. In this iteration , that landed them right behind the Chiefs at No. 13 and ahead of the Cowboys at No. 15. Along with the rankings, each team’s beat writer also added in a “milestone to watch for” this season in regards one of the players. Kris Rhim highlighted that, at some point this season, quarterback Justin Herbert could become just the fourth passer in league history to throw for over 28,000 during their first seven seasons. The other three being Peyton Manning (29,442), Patrick Mahomes (28,424), and Matt Ryan (28,166). “Herbert has thrown fewer than the 3,180 yards he needs to reach 28K just once in his career,” said Rhim. “That year was 2023, when he sustained a season-ending injury to his right index finger but still threw for 3,134 yards in 13 games. With new offensive coordinator Mike McDaniel, barring any injury, Herbert should have one of the most productive seasons of his career and reach this mark late in the season. ” After a couple seasons where it simply felt like Herbert was being hamstrung by an offense that wanted to run, run, run, it may be time for him to get back to the type of play that we were awestruck by from 2020-2022 where he totaled over 14,000 passing yards and 102 total touchdowns. Now THAT’S what we’ve all been missing. So why couldn’t happen under McDaniel in 2026? Wish I remember which podcast I heard it on, but apparently Mike McDaniel told Jim Harbaugh that there are concepts in his passing game that he's never been able to use because you need a "freak" at QB. And when Justin Herbert demonstrated said freakiness at practice, McDaniel… https://t.co/edOGIpOIM9 — Dhruv Koul (@DhruvKoul) August 28, 2026

title: Los Angeles Chargers 53-man roster: Analyzing the initial team, including 2 UDFAs who made it
summary: The Chargers announced their initial 53-man roster around 6:00 p.m. Sunday evening. It came with several notable surprises, including having only two specialists and 11 total offensive linemen. Below is a complete breakdown of the roster along with some analysis on each room. Quarterback (2): Justin Herbert, Trey Lance Even as someone who believes D.J. […]
full_text: INGLEWOOD, CA - AUGUST 27: Jacob Spomer #60 of the Los Angeles Chargers on the sidelines during an NFL preseason game between the Los Angeles Rams and the Los Angeles Chargers on August 27, 2026, at SoFi Stadium in Inglewood, California. (Photo by Greg Fiore/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Chargers announced their initial 53-man roster around 6:00 p.m. Sunday evening. It came with several notable surprises, including having only two specialists and 11 total offensive linemen. Below is a complete breakdown of the roster along with some analysis on each room. Quarterback (2): Justin Herbert, Trey Lance Even as someone who believes D.J. Uiagalelei outplayed Lance during the preseason by a decent margin, the Chargers were always going to keep Lance as their backup due to his larger pool of experience in the NFL, on top of his familiarity with the Shanahan-influenced offense that Mike McDaniel wants to run (even if he’s not the best at executing it himself). Uiagalelei is expected to return on the team’s practice squad for another year, but the Chargers would be wise to still look elsewhere for an upgrade at backup behind Herbert. Former 49ers quarterback Nick Mullens was released and he has even more experience in running this style of offense than Lance during the former’s time with the 49ers. Running back (3): Omarion Hampton, Keaton Mitchell, Kimani Vidal Both Amar Johnson and Greg DesRosiers Jr. performed well enough to make the final roster, but positional needs elsewhere forced the Chargers to keep this group nice and tight. Hampton will rightfully lead the team in carries while Mitchell’s speed and complementary skillset gets rotated in given the situation. Vidal rushed for over 100 yards three times in 2025 and had another game with 95. His skillset fits well enough as a north-south runner who can eek out extra yards through contact. It also helps that he showed the ability to be a lead rusher behind that abomination of a 2025 offensive line. Fullback (1): Alec Ingold No surprises here. The Chargers got the perfect fullback for Mike McDaniels’ offense and I’m actually thoroughly excited to see Ingold in action this season. He’ll be pivotal in unlocking Hampton into one of the league’s best ball-carriers. Wide Receivers (6): Ladd McConkey, Quentin Johnston, Tre’ Harris, Brenen Thompson, Derius Davis, KeAndre Lambert-Smith The Chargers chose to keep KeAndre Lambert-Smith after another sollid preseason where he showed good rapport with the Chargers’ backup quarterbacks. KLS is a NFL wide receiver and you could do far worse for the team’s WR5. Davis makes the team as the presumed return man. He was used on an end-around against the Rams that went for a big gain so there may be a chance he gets back into the offense thanks to McDaniel. However, there’s still so many mouths to feed in this offense and rookie Brenen Thompson — who has comparable speed — is a much better overall wideout than Davis. The biggest question here is how the top three will shake out in terms of usage. I think the safe bet is McConkey will be “the guy” but Harris has looked phenomenal this summer while also being the best run blocker at receiver. He’ll potentially lead the whole position in snaps played if McDaniel is truly a believer in “no block, no rock.” Tight End (3): Charlie Kolar, David Njoku, Oronde Gadsden II Kolar caught two passes this preseason while playing amongst the starters who overall got single-digit snaps together as a group. That’s good efficiency for a guy labeled as the “blocking tight end” when they first signed him. He’s a sneaky pick to lead this group is receptions, even with Gadsden and Njoku in the same room. Both Gadsden and Njoku also have to become more consistent as run blockers, as well. Neither player looked comfortable blocking on the move this preseason and they were directly related to why their only drive against the Niners was a three-and-out. Offensive Line (11): Rashawn Slater, Joe Alt, Jake Slaughter, Cole Strange, Kayode Awosika, Trey Pipkins, Jacob Spomer, Travis Burke, Logan Taylor, Alex Harkey, Trevor Penning The Chargers held on to several players here that I do no agree with, but the placement of Branson Taylor on IR designated to return left them an extra spot. But they kept three (3) names here I did not expect them to hold onto. We all know what Penning is. It was not a successful move when they traded for him at the deadline last season. Harkey and Taylor both did not standout in the preseason, but Taylor at least spent most of the time at tackle which is the position we did not expect him to play in the NFL. He was the one of the three I expected to be kept, if any of them. Plenty of players they cut would have been preferred over either of Penning or Harkey. I don’t get it. Interior Defenders (5): Teair Tart, Dalvin Tomlinson, Jamaree Caldwell, Justin Eboigbe, Nick Barrett After a standout preseason, the Chargers chose to get some worth out of TeRah Edwards whom they did not expect to be kept on the final 53. He was sent to the Panthers for a sixth-round pick in 2028. This group is otherwise as expected. You have the starters, the veteran free-agent signing, and the rookie. Good depth and a solid group overal. Edge Rushers (4): Khalil Mack, Tuli Tuipulotu, Bud Dupree, Akheem Mesidor After neither Nadame Tucker and Kyle Kennard impressed enough to force their way here, the Chargers are moving ahead with their best four. No frills here. Just a strong group with high expectations, especially for their first-rounder in Mesidor. Linebackers (5): Denzel Perryman, Daiyan Henley, Troy Dye, Marlowe Wax, Del’Shawn Phillips Marlowe Wax was phenomenal in August and that stamped his ticket to the active roster. Phillips obviously makes the team after a Second-Team All-Pro honor as a special-teamer. This group is nothing flashy, but it’s solid and has been what the defense has needed to be a top-five unit each of the past two seasons. Cornerbacks (5): Donte Jackson, Tarheeb Still, Cam Hart, Deane Leondard, Rodney Shelley With a ton of competition past the top four cornerbacks, Shelley was the guy who came out on top to make the roster as CB5. Avery Smith, whom many thought was a roster lock, was shipped to the Seahawks for a 2027 sixth-round pick. I truly hope the Chargers don’t regret that decision. He seemed like a potential future starter when Jackson’s time with the team was done. Safeties (6): Derwin James, Elijah Molden, Tony Jefferson, R.J. Mickens, Genesis Smith, Kendall Williamson Williamson was always going to be kept due to his contriutions on special teams. That made it tough for the Chargers not to keep six players at safety. Since James has been the teams primary nickel defender, it made it more palatable to keep five cornerbacks. Mickens remains a special teams contrubutor, as well, and Smith was one of their fourth-round picks. They round out a solid group with “Unc” (Jefferson) who had a hilarious cut day going from out to making the roster in the few hours before the deadline. Special Teams (2): Cameron Dicker, Josh Harris The Chargers released punter JK Scott and for five minutes there was a massive moment of rejoice within fan base. However, that was short-lived until NFL insiders began reporting that the intent of the Chargers was to bring him back, similarly to when they started the 2025 season with only two specialist before signing a long snapper. I don’t see what the teams sees anymore with Scott. He’s wildly inconsistent and those inconsistencies tend to show their head in some of the worst moments possible. It’s HARD to shank a punt 20 yards when trying your best. It’s also hard to follow that with a 33-yard punt in the same game. That’s horrendous for a high school or college punter, nonetheless a professional who has been in the league for almost a decade. The Chargers need to find competition now, not after the season.
